To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the PCM method is a reliable method of asbestos exposure monitoring; (2) the PCM method has limitations in resolution and the counting rules used, which underestimates the asbestos fiber concentration; (3) asbestos fibers are present in the air in buildings containing ACM; (4) the presence of asbestos does not necessarily imply exposure; and (5) exposure depends on the physical condition and the type of maintenance and operating program in place.
asbestos fibers are ubiquitous in buildings, that asbestos exposure in nonindustrial buildings is low, and that the risk to the occupants of buildings with ACM is low.
asbestos exposure in nonindustrial buildings may be underestimated by PCM and that a survey by a trained professional is needed to determine whether the asbestos is in a condition to become airborne.

the development of new analytical methods for the detection, quantitation, and identification of asbestos fibers in air samples.
the assessment and control of asbestos exposure in nonindustrial environments.

there is a need for the use of the TEM method to accurately determine asbestos exposure levels in the workplace.

asbestos exposure in office and commercial settings can be minimized by a thorough survey of the building and the implementation of an appropriate maintenance plan to ensure that ACM are not disturbed.

asbestos is a problem in the environment, especially in buildings.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PCM method of asbestos fiber analysis is not a reliable indicator of the actual airborne asbestos concentration in a building.
the current asbestos exposure assessment methods are not sufficient to assess asbestos fiber exposure in non-industrial settings.
the use of PCM analysis to monitor asbestos in buildings is not adequate to ensure that the occupants are not exposed to airborne asbestos fibers.
